title: On measures of influence and discordance in phylogenomic analyses
content:
Abstract
As models are approximate descriptions of real biological processes, and data are collected often with errors and contamination, sensitivity or robustness of phylogenomic and population genomic analyses to perturbations to the data or the likelihood model is important. Here we review ideas in sensitivity analyses developed in the statistics literature. Global methods introduce changes to data points (such as deleting one or a group of data points) or the likelihood model to assess the impact of the perturbation on the model’s fit to data or on estimation of parameters. The analysis may identify outlier observations or influential data points. Local methods mostly use derivatives to assess the impact of local perturbations around the standard analysis. In the Bayesian framework, similar approaches have been developed to assess the sensitivity of Bayesian inference to the prior, the likelihood model, and the data. We use an example of linear regression to introduce major concepts and illustrate them using problems in phylogenomics. We argue that examination of sensitivity and robustness is at least as important as the fit of the model to data in phylogenetic analysis.
